lessons.title: What nematodes are and how they harm crops
lessons.html:
What nematodes are and how they harm crops

Nematodes (eelworms) are tiny worms that live in the soil. Most are too small to see without a microscope. Some kinds attack plant roots. They are a big problem in crops such as potatoes, tomatoes, vegetables, sugarcane, bananas and citrus.

How nematodes harm plants

Root-knot nematodes enter roots and make swellings called galls or knots. Damaged roots cannot take up water and food properly. The plant then:

  • grows slowly and stays small;
  • turns yellow;
  • wilts in the heat of the day, even when the soil is wet;
  • gives a small harvest.

Damage often shows up in patches in the field, not across the whole land.

How to check for nematodes

  1. Look for patches of weak, yellow or wilting plants.
  2. Carefully dig out a plant with its roots. Do not pull it.
  3. Shake off the soil gently and look at the roots.
  4. Knots and swellings on the roots are a sign of root-knot nematodes.
  5. Report it to your supervisor. The farm may send soil and root samples to a laboratory to confirm the type and number of nematodes.

Ways to control nematodes

  • Crop rotation: do not plant the same kind of crop in the same land every season.
  • Clean planting material: use certified, clean seedlings and seed cane.
  • Clean tools and tyres: nematodes move with soil on boots, spades and tractor wheels.
  • Resistant cultivars where available.
  • Nematicides: chemicals that kill nematodes. These are used when the farm manager decides, based on samples and advice.

Nematicides can be very poisonous. Only trained workers may apply them, under supervision. The next lesson explains how.

lessons.title: Applying nematicides safely by hand
lessons.html:
Applying nematicides safely by hand

Nematicides are agricultural remedies. In South Africa they must be registered under Act 36 of 1947 and used exactly as the label says. Many nematicides are highly toxic to people, animals and birds.

Before you start

  • Your supervisor must tell you which product, how much, where and how to apply it.
  • Read or have someone read the label to you. The label gives the dose, the PPE needed, first aid and the waiting period before people may enter the land or before harvest. Follow the product label.
  • Check your PPE: chemical-resistant gloves, overalls, rubber boots, face shield or goggles, and a respirator if the label says so.
  • Check that the measuring cup, applicator or knapsack sprayer is clean and not leaking.

Applying the product

  1. Measure the dose exactly with the measuring cup or calibrated applicator. Never guess and never use your hands.
  2. Apply granules into the planting furrow or around the plant as instructed, then cover with soil straight away so birds and animals cannot eat them.
  3. For liquid products, mix only in the place your supervisor shows you, never near a water source, and apply as instructed.
  4. Work with the wind behind you. Do not apply in strong wind.
  5. Do not eat, drink or smoke while working.

After applying

  • Clean equipment at the chosen wash area, away from rivers and dams.
  • Return leftover product to the locked chemical store. Never take it home.
  • Do not reuse empty containers; handle them as the label and farm rules say.
  • Wash gloves before taking them off, then wash your hands, face and body. Change clothes.
  • Put up warning signs if required and record the product, amount, date and land.

If someone is poisoned

Signs can include headache, dizziness, sweating, vomiting, blurred vision or trouble breathing. Move the person away from the chemical, remove contaminated clothing, wash the skin with lots of clean water and get medical help immediately. Take the label or container with you to the clinic. Follow the first aid on the label.

Key points

  • Nematodes damage roots and cause stunted, yellow, wilting plants.
  • Rotation, clean plants and clean tools help prevent them.
  • Use nematicides only when trained and supervised, exactly as the label says.
  • Always wear the PPE on the label and cover granules with soil.
  • If poisoning happens, wash off the chemical and get medical help with the label.
